evidence_originality: A unified automatic logging layer or wrapper is the standard, expected response to a logging mandate and is mundane.

evidence_acceptability: Automated logging for compliance is a common, norm-conforming strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: An internal API wrapper over existing ML pipelines is a reasonably feasible engineering effort requiring some changes but no radical restructuring.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by recording events automatically.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic event logging would meet the Article 12 logging mandate in part, but it lacks detail on required content (Article 12(2)-(3)), retention, and traceability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized automated logging/observability libraries are a standard, expected response to logging mandates, so the idea is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a library/wrapper) but still treats compliance as logging practice, deliberately decoupling it from the science.
evidence_acceptability: A standardized internal logging library integrated into CI/CD is a common engineering strategy that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a modular API wrapper and integrating it into existing pipelines requires some engineering changes but is reasonably feasible, not trivial across all model architectures.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate (do X to get automated compliant logs) while minimizing burden on R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: Automated event and I/O capture would contribute substantially to meeting Article 12 logging, but it does not address specifics such as Article 12(2) event relevance, retention, or Annex III items, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Privacy-preserving logging is a fairly well-known idea, though applying differential privacy to Article 12 logs is somewhat interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (differential privacy, hashing) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-protecting logs are a sensible, norm-respecting strategy, though anonymizing the identities of verifying persons may sit uneasily with Article 12(3)(d) and is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: Cryptographic hashing is routine, but applying differential privacy to audit logs while keeping them verifiable requires some changes and nontrivial engineering, so it is reasonably feasible but not trivial.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets how to meet the logging mandate while avoiding privacy conflicts, an identified problem tied to the stated compliance decision.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps reconcile logging with privacy but is only a partial solution, since it does not cover the full logging mandate and anonymizing required identifications could undermine traceability.

evidence_originality: Internal mock-audit and log verification tools are a fairly expected response to logging mandates, though the decision-path reconstruction is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal introduces a new element (an internal audit simulation dashboard) but still treats compliance as a logging-validation practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: An internal self-audit tool violates no legal or social norms and is a common compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: Building an aggregation dashboard that cross-references logs, model versions, inputs and verifier identities requires moderate engineering but is reasonably feasible with existing tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified need to confirm Article 12 logging compliance (do X to validate traceability, which is part of the stated problem).
evidence_effectiveness: It would verify that logging is sufficient and traceable but does not itself create the logging capability or address broader R&D adaptation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging layer for compliance is a common, expected response with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging infrastructure that leaves the lab's R&D and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized compliance tooling is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a shared logging API on existing compute clusters requires some pipeline changes and engineering effort but is reasonably feasible with standard tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by automating timestamps, session durations, and data references named in Article 12.
evidence_effectiveness: A centralized logging module would, if built, deliver the automatic event recording Article 12 requires, but it is vague on Article 12(2) event relevance, retention, and the Annex III 1(a) specifics, so it is a substantial but partial solution.

evidence_originality: Auto-generating living technical documentation from CI/CD and experiment metadata is an interesting, fairly expected tooling response (similar to model cards/MLOps practice), showing modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling and process (dynamic documentation pipeline) but still treats compliance as documentation/logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Automated documentation is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms or laws.
evidence_implementability: Integrating existing CI/CD, version control, and metadata stores with documentation generators is reasonably feasible with some engineering effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Recital 71 technical documentation and traceability need, but Article 12's event logging over the system's lifetime is only implied, so it solves a related rather than the core logging problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help keep documentation current and traceable but does not itself provide the automatic event logs of deployed systems required by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A centralized logging library is a common, mundane response that evaluators would expect from most labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, with no change to how the lab's R&D relates to its obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Building an internal compliance logging library is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Integrating middleware across diverse model architectures and all high-risk pipelines requires some engineering effort and changes but is reasonably feasible with existing techniques.
evidence_applicability: A standardized logging library directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the Article 12 automatic event-recording mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared middleware that automatically captures timestamps and state changes would substantially meet the logging mandate, but it is vague about which events (risk situations, post-market monitoring, Annex III minimums such as reference database and human verifier identity) are recorded, so it is mostly but not fully a solution.

evidence_originality: Risk-triage of projects against the Act's categories is an obvious, common first step that most labs would propose.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance scoping practice that leaves the lab's way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Risk-based classification under Annex III is a standard, legally grounded compliance strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A triage rubric and classification review of existing R&D pipelines needs some process effort but no radical technical change, so it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of deciding how to respond and where to allocate logging resources under the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Classification only scopes where logging is required and does not itself deliver the logging capability, so it contributes only partially to the solution.

evidence_originality: A standardized internal logging library or API wrapper is the most common, expected response a lab would give to a logging mandate, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as ordinary logging practice via centralized tooling and leaves the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized internal logging tooling is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Building an internal library with a core engineering team that integrates with existing infrastructure is a reasonably standard, feasible engineering effort with moderate cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 automatic event-recording mandate across the lab's high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver the automatic logging capability, but it lacks specifics on which events are logged (Article 12(2) traceability purposes, Annex III requirements, retention), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Internal rotating peer audits against a regulatory checklist are a common, expected response, with little surprise or imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: An internal peer-review audit of documentation against a checklist is standard compliance practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal audits and peer reviews are a conventional strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Monthly reviews by rotating senior researchers need no new tools or hires and are low cost, though they take some researcher time.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of verifying that records and documentation are adequate, which relates to but is not the direct logging mandate (Recital 71 documentation versus Article 12 automatic logs).
evidence_effectiveness: It reviews documentation and logs for gaps but does not itself build automatic event logging required by Article 12, so it only partially contributes to compliance.

evidence_originality: Using regulatory logs as a research substrate for interpretability is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, though counterfactual analysis and attention mapping are standard techniques.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It weaves the compliance logs into the lab's interpretability research and publication, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, but it does not rethink what the lab researches overall.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing methods and aligning research with regulatory needs offends no norms and is a reasonable, somewhat uncommon strategy.
evidence_implementability: The lab can apply existing interpretability methods to log data with moderate effort, though sparse logs may limit what can be reconstructed, so some changes and uncertainty are involved.
evidence_applicability: The proposal aims to use Article 12 logs to identify risk triggers and support post-market monitoring, which directly relates to the logging mandate's purposes in Article 12(2), though it does not itself specify how to implement the logging.
evidence_effectiveness: Reconstructing decision paths from sparse logs would help with risk identification and monitoring but is only a partial solution since it does not ensure logging capability is built, and sparse logs may not support attention mapping or counterfactuals without model access.

evidence_originality: A centralized shared logging library capturing timestamps, hashes and version metadata is the most common, expected engineering response to Article 12, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice that leaves the lab's R&D approach and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A standardized, mandatory internal logging library is a common compliance strategy that violates no norms, though mandating it for all research code may cause minor friction.
evidence_implementability: Building a shared library and making it a mandatory dependency requires some engineering changes and integration across diverse projects, but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate, explicitly targeting Article 12(1) automatic event recording.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic logging of every inference would satisfy Article 12(1) but does not cover the Article 12(2) purposes or the Annex III 1(a) minimum fields such as reference database, matched inputs, and verifier identity, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Separating regulatory log archives onto immutable storage is a sensible and fairly common infrastructure response, interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A dedicated immutable-ledger log archive is a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging/storage practice separate from research, leaving the lab's way of working largely unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Segregated immutable log storage is a conventional, norm-compliant approach that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a separate scalable storage tier with immutable ledger requires budget and engineering effort but is reasonably feasible with existing technologies.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12 mandate for retaining automatically recorded event logs over the system lifetime, though it covers storage rather than what to log.
evidence_effectiveness: Storage and retention is only one part of compliance (event definition, traceability content, Annex III specifics are not addressed), so it contributes partially to a solution.

evidence_originality: A unified logging framework with an immutable layer in shared libraries is a common, expected engineering response to Article 12.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A standardized logging API in base libraries is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, apart from researchers calling a few functions.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized, standardized logging is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a shared logging library and requiring researchers to call it is reasonably feasible with some engineering effort and modest workflow changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by producing automatic event logs across high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute substantially to compliance, but it does not specify which events to log, retention, or Annex III minimum fields, and relies on researchers calling functions, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Applying anomaly detection to logs for drift detection is interesting and somewhat imaginative, but it is a fairly expected idea in the AI monitoring space.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance logs as a source of scientific research and safety tooling, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Using mandatory logs for safety research violates no norms, though privacy and data-use constraints need care.
evidence_implementability: Statistical anomaly detection on existing logs is feasible with moderate effort, though it needs data, high-resolution logging, and research staff.
evidence_applicability: Using logs to detect substantial modifications and risk situations ties directly to Article 12(2)(a) and post-market monitoring, though it is framed as a research project rather than a compliance method, so it addresses an implied problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Anomaly detection on logs would help identify drift and risks, but it does not itself deliver the logging mandate, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Using an auxiliary AI monitor to scan logs for drift is a fairly expected and interesting response, with some imagination in framing compliance as a safety research opportunity but not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (an automated monitoring model) and gestures at turning compliance into research, but it still essentially treats compliance as logging practice layered with a tool.
evidence_acceptability: Log-monitoring tools violate no norms or laws and are a common, accepted strategy in compliance and safety work.
evidence_implementability: A small team training a lightweight monitor on existing failure datasets is reasonably feasible, though defining and validating drift detection takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of identifying risk/substantial modification situations in Article 12(2)(a), which relates to but does not directly meet the core logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help use logs for risk identification and monitoring but does not itself ensure automatic event recording or the Article 12(3) minimum content, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A unified logging library with decorators is a common, expected response to a logging mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: This is standard compliance logging practice with a shared library, leaving the lab's way of working and relationship between R&D and compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Standard internal compliance tooling violates no norms or sensibilities and is a common strategy.
evidence_implementability: Building a modular logging library with APIs and decorators is a common engineering task requiring some changes to researcher code and a central database, so it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The library directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 automatic event-logging mandate by capturing events, timestamps and inputs/matches.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, centralized standardized logging would largely satisfy the logging mandate, though it is generic and does not detail which events satisfy Article 12(2) relevance or retention and so is slightly short of a full solution.

evidence_originality: Automated compliance tests for logging in CI is a sensible but fairly common DevOps-style response that an experienced evaluator would expect from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (compliance probes in CI) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing of compliance features in CI is a common, uncontroversial practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building simulation probes and integrating them into an existing CI pipeline requires some new development but is reasonably feasible with standard engineering tools.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets verifying that the Article 12(3) mandatory logging data points are captured, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It verifies and catches gaps in logging but does not itself build the logging capability or address Article 12(1)-(2) broader traceability, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A verification portal with digital signatures for reviewers is a fairly predictable, mundane way to satisfy the Article 12(3)(d) requirement to identify the people who verify results.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, with a sign-off tool added and the lab's R&D and its relationship to compliance left unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Digital sign-off and audit trails for human reviewers are common, legally sensible practices that violate no norms, though some reviewer-monitoring concerns may arise.
evidence_implementability: Building a verification portal with digital signatures and gating the system's task completion on sign-off needs moderate development and workflow integration but is reasonably feasible with existing technology.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified requirement of recording the natural persons involved in verification under Article 12(3)(d), which is part of the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would satisfy only 12(3)(d), which applies to Annex III 1(a) systems, and leaves the general logging in 12(1)-(2) and the other 12(3) items (use periods, reference database, matched inputs) unaddressed, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated experiment tracking and model cards from CI/CD are common, expected responses, so the idea is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tooling/automation element but still treats compliance as documentation and logging practice without changing the R&D-compliance relationship.
evidence_acceptability: Automated documentation generation in CI/CD is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Exporting hyperparameters, dataset versions, and metrics from a CI/CD pipeline on each commit uses standard MLOps tooling and is low-cost with non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified need to keep technical documentation up to date from Recital 71, which is related to but not the core Article 12 event-logging mandate, so it addresses an implied problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help meet the technical documentation requirement but does not implement the automatic event logging mandated by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Content-addressable storage and cryptographic hashing for dataset versioning is a well-known MLOps practice (e.g., DVC, lakeFS), so it is common rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a data versioning tool but treats compliance as standard traceability/logging practice without changing how the lab does R&D.
evidence_acceptability: Data versioning and hashing are common, uncontroversial strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Off-the-shelf versioning and hashing tools exist, so adoption requires some workflow changes but is reasonably feasible at moderate cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses traceability of training data, which relates to Article 12's traceability purpose and Recital 71, but Article 12 concerns runtime event logs rather than dataset versioning, so the problem solved is only implied.
evidence_effectiveness: Dataset versioning would help documentation and traceability but does not deliver the automatic event logging over system lifetime that Article 12 mandates, so it is only a partial solution and overstated as definitive evidence.

evidence_originality: Validating logs through testing is a fairly expected response, though the adversarial risk-scenario framing adds a little interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a test suite) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Testing logging adequacy before regulatory review is a sensible, uncontroversial compliance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building adversarial scenario tests and trace-completeness checks requires some new tooling and effort but is reasonably feasible with existing engineering skills.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of ensuring logs capture events relevant to risk identification under Article 12(2), which is part of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help verify that logs meet Article 12(2) traceability but does not itself implement logging or cover the whole mandate, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Living documentation with cryptographic linking of datasets, validation and risk assessments to model weights is somewhat imaginative, but versioned model/data lineage and documentation automation is a fairly expected response among AI labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (version-controlled, cryptographically linked records) and merges scientific reporting with compliance documentation, yet still treats compliance as a documentation/record practice rather than changing what the lab researches or its relationship to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Documentation pipelines and provenance tracking violate no norms and are uncontroversial for regulators and scientists alike.
evidence_implementability: Version control, data/model lineage tools, and hashing are mature, so this is reasonably feasible with some changes to workflows and tooling integration, though not trivial.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the related documentation and traceability need implied by the Act rather than the stated logging mandate itself (automatic event recording over system lifetime), so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially help with technical documentation and traceability (Recital 71), but it does not directly address Article 12's automatic event logging of runtime operation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Anomaly-triggered logging is a common, expected response to Article 12(2)(a) and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds telemetry probes and thresholds but still treats compliance purely as a logging practice without changing how the lab works.
evidence_acceptability: Event-triggered logging for risk situations is a conventional, legally aligned approach that offends no norms, though minimal logging outside anomalies might raise audit questions.
evidence_implementability: Telemetry probes with threshold-triggered logging are standard engineering that require some added modules but no radical change, though defining the thresholds takes effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate by recording events relevant to identifying risk situations under Article 12(2)(a).
evidence_effectiveness: It covers only the risk-identification part of Article 12 and may miss the continuous logging, post-market monitoring, and Annex III minimum logging requirements, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compressed log formats and selective sampling for efficient logging is a fairly expected response from labs, with little that is surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new technical methods (compressed formats, sampling) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, though it frames it as research.
evidence_acceptability: Reducing logging overhead is a common strategy, but selective sampling could raise legal concerns about completeness; it still offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: A focused R&D project on log compression is feasible with existing engineering skills, though selective sampling that keeps legal traceability needs some effort and research.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by making logging efficient, though it addresses cost and performance more than the mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help to meet the mandate cheaply but is only a partial solution, as it does not define what to log, and sampling risks undermining Article 12 traceability.

evidence_originality: Centralized ML experiment tracking and provenance logging is a very common, expected response to such a mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a standard middleware tool but still treats compliance as logging practice, with reproducibility as a side benefit rather than a changed relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Automated logging for compliance and reproducibility is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Integrating a unified logging API into an internal ML pipeline requires some engineering changes but is reasonably feasible with existing tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by implementing automated event recording in the lab's pipeline.
evidence_effectiveness: A unified logging middleware capturing runtime events and timestamps would substantially meet the Article 12 automatic-recording mandate, but it focuses on training metadata and experiments rather than deployed-system logs, post-market monitoring, or Annex III-specific items, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Auto-generating compliance documentation from Git and MLflow metadata is a fairly common MLOps practice that many labs would propose, so it is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a pipeline and reporting template) but still treats compliance as documentation/logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Automating documentation from existing development tools is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Integrating Git and MLflow metadata via a Python script with a template is low cost and uses existing tooling with non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses technical documentation and record-keeping from Recital 71, which is related to but not the same as the Article 12 automatic event logging mandate, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with technical documentation but does not provide runtime event logging of the deployed system required by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: An authenticated sign-off portal with SSO and timestamped logs is a common, expected response to human-oversight logging requirements.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance tooling response that treats the mandate as a logging practice and does not change how the lab's R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Authenticated reviewer sign-off with audit trails is a conventional strategy that violates no norms, though the logging of identifiable individuals has minor data-protection considerations.
evidence_implementability: Building an SSO-gated review interface linked to event logs uses well-established technology and requires moderate, non-radical development effort.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets Article 12(3)(d) by linking the identity of verifying natural persons to event logs for Annex III 1(a) systems, which is an identified part of the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If built, the portal would satisfy the verifier-identification and timestamp requirement, but it covers only one part of Article 12 (not the use period, reference database, or matched input data logging), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reusable logging middleware with a single config flag is a mundane, expected response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, even reducing overhead for researchers.
evidence_acceptability: Shared logging middleware is a common, uncontroversial engineering and compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A reusable library with decorators and hooks integrated into one core framework is a reasonably feasible engineering effort requiring some changes but no radical restructuring.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate across the lab's high-risk prototypes (do X to get automatic logs).
evidence_effectiveness: Standardized middleware capturing inputs, outputs, and session durations would substantially deliver the automatic logging mandate, but it omits event relevance for risk identification, reference database and match data, and human verifier identification, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A standardized logging library and API wrapper is a mundane, expected response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized compliance tooling for logging is a common, uncontroversial engineering strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building an API wrapper into existing deployment pipelines is a reasonably feasible measure that needs some engineering work but no radical change.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem by building a shared logging library for automatic event recording, including usage periods and reference databases that Article 12 requires.
evidence_effectiveness: A unified logging wrapper would meet much of the Article 12(1) and 12(3) logging mandate, but it does not cover the event relevance for risk identification, post-market monitoring, or the identification of verifying persons, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Studying UI/UX for verifier attribution and the effect of logging overhead on human accuracy is an interesting angle but not highly surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (HCI user studies) yet still treats compliance as logging practice for Article 12(3)(d), so it only slightly stretches the paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: User studies with domain experts and identity logging of verifiers are lawful, conventional research practices that offend no norms, though verifier identification raises minor privacy considerations.
evidence_implementability: Running user studies and integrating identity verification into a review pipeline requires some changes and recruiting experts but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the Article 12(3)(d) requirement to identify natural persons verifying results, which is part of the stated logging mandate, though only for one narrow provision.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help meet one sub-requirement and reduce human-accuracy costs of logging, but it is only a partial solution to the overall logging mandate and applies only to Annex III 1(a) systems.

evidence_originality: A standardized internal logging library is the mundane, expected response that most labs would propose.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance purely as standard logging practice via a shared tool, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A centralized shared logging library is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a modular API and secure archive requires some engineering and researcher integration effort, but it is a reasonably feasible, standard software project.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by automatically capturing timestamps, inputs, and user IDs.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would deliver automatic event recording across systems, but it covers only basic telemetry and not Annex III-specific items, risk-situation identification, or retention and documentation, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using NLP to translate logs into human-readable rationales and flag risk patterns is interesting and somewhat imaginative, though explainability and log analytics are fairly familiar directions.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (NLP-based log interpretation) and ties compliance to an explainability research agenda, but it still treats compliance essentially as logging practice rather than changing the R&D-compliance relationship.
evidence_acceptability: Research on log interpretability is a conventional, non-offensive undertaking that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A research initiative to develop new NLP methods for interpreting logs requires significant effort and uncertain results, which is hard to commit scarce implementation resources to, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (making logs useful for risk identification and monitoring under Art. 12(2)) related to the mandate, while conflating logs with the 'comprehensible information' of Recital 71 that concerns technical documentation.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with traceability and risk identification from logs but does not itself ensure that the Article 12 logging capability and required record contents exist, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Tiered hot/cold storage for compliance logs is a standard, mundane IT approach that most labs would propose.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging infrastructure practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Separating and tiering compliance data is a common strategy that violates no norms or legal sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Tiered storage with automatic lifecycle policies is mature, uses existing capacity, and is low-cost with non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (cost-effective retention of logs over the system lifetime) that relates to the logging mandate rather than the core requirement of enabling automatic event recording.
evidence_effectiveness: Tiered storage for retained logs and documentation helps meet lifetime retention, but it does not address what events get logged, traceability content, or the Article 12(2)-(3) minimum logging capabilities, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Provenance tracking for ML is known, and the dual-use framing is interesting and shows some imagination but is not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (graph-based provenance) and explicitly reframes compliance record-keeping as a scientific asset improving reproducibility, which shifts the relationship between R&D and compliance somewhat.
evidence_acceptability: Version-controlled metadata tracking and human-readable regulatory reports are common, norm-respecting practices in MLOps and compliance.
evidence_implementability: Graph-based tracking of every pipeline mutation requires building or integrating new tooling and changes to workflows, but it is reasonably feasible with existing experiment-tracking tools.
evidence_applicability: It addresses traceability and technical documentation of training pipelines, which is closely tied to the record-keeping mandate, though Article 12 specifically concerns automatic event logs of system operation rather than development provenance, so the link is implied rather than direct.
evidence_effectiveness: Provenance graphs would help with traceability and documentation (Recital 71) but do not cover runtime event logging, risk-situation identification, or Annex III minimum logging fields, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Cryptographic verifiable logging with zero-knowledge proofs is an interesting and somewhat imaginative idea, but privacy-preserving audit logs are a known research area and not highly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (ZK proofs, MPC-based blind audit trails) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, though it also frames the work as a research agenda, which keeps it at slight stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Regulators and the lab would find privacy-preserving auditable logging acceptable and non-offensive, though ZK-based audit is somewhat unusual for regulators to accept.
evidence_implementability: Developing ZKP/MPC protocols for AI event logs is a difficult, expensive research effort with uncertain outcome, and the stated approval context requires committing implementation resources rather than exploring, so it is significantly hard but not impossible.
