evidence_acceptability: Automating documentation from Git and MLflow is a common, legally unobjectionable compliance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Scraping Git and MLflow metadata into templates uses existing tooling and needs only modest integration work, though template mapping takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the documentation burden, which is related to the regulation but only implied by the logging mandate in the stated problem, and it conflates experiment logs with system event logs.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help produce technical documentation (Recital 71) but does not address the Article 12 automatic event logging of the AI system itself, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Docs-as-code and automated compliance documentation are fairly well-known ideas, making this interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (automated dossier generation) but still treats compliance as a documentation practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automating compliance documentation from experiment trackers is a sensible, non-controversial practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Integrating experiment trackers with documentation generation takes some engineering and process changes but uses existing tools and is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the technical documentation and keep-up-to-date requirement from Recital 71, which relates to the record-keeping mandate, but it does not directly address Article 12's event logging, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Automated documentation helps keep technical records current, but it does not provide automatic event logs or the Article 12(2)-(3) logging capabilities, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Auto-generating documentation from experiment tracking and Git is an interesting and fairly expected idea, not especially surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as a documentation and logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automating documentation from version control is a common, norm-compliant strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Integrating Git metadata and experiment trackers into a documentation generator uses existing tools and is reasonably feasible, though it needs some engineering work.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the documentation upkeep of Recital 71, which is related to the logging mandate but is an implied problem rather than the Article 12 logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help keep technical documentation current, but it does not address Article 12 event logging itself, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Auto-generating compliance documentation from experiment-tracking tools is a fairly common, expected response, though the immutable scientific record framing adds mild interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (template engine pipeline) but still treats compliance as a documentation/logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated documentation generation is a common strategy that violates no norms or laws.
evidence_implementability: It builds on existing experiment tracking software plus a template engine, so it needs modest changes at reasonable cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the documentation and record-keeping need directly, but Article 12 concerns automatic event logs of the deployed system rather than R&D technical documentation, so it solves a related implied problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with technical documentation (Recital 71, Article 11) but does not provide the runtime event logging Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Risk-tier classification of projects is a common, expected first step for labs responding to the AI Act, so it is mundane rather than imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A decision-matrix tagging tool is a new process element, but it still treats compliance as standard logging/classification practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Internal risk classification is a common, norm-compliant compliance strategy that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A decision matrix and tagging process built on Annex III criteria is cheap and requires only modest process changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (determining which systems must meet Article 12 logging) that relates to the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate efficiently.
evidence_effectiveness: Triage of which systems need logging helps scope the effort but does not itself implement logging capabilities, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Auto-generating documentation from Git hooks and build metadata is a common, expected compliance-tooling response (docs-as-code, model cards), so it is mundane rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool and pipeline but still treats compliance as documentation/logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automated documentation pipelines are a common strategy that offends no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Git hooks, config files, and templated generation are standard, low-cost tooling that fits existing build workflows with non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly solves an identified problem (keeping technical documentation up to date per Recital 71), which is related to but not the core logging mandate of the stated problem, so it addresses an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help keep technical documentation current but does not address Article 12's automatic event logging (logs of use, reference databases, input data), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Building a log dashboard or reporting layer on ELK is a common, mundane response that an evaluator would expect from most labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: An ELK-based dashboard is a standard tooling layer that treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D workflow unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal audit dashboards on standard log stacks are a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: ELK or similar tooling is mature and readily deployable with modest engineering effort and little disruption to core development, though report design and log schema work require some changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, making recorded logs usable for traceability and post-market monitoring (Recital 71), which relates to but is not the core logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: A log query and reporting portal helps make logs comprehensible and usable for audit and monitoring, but it does not itself make the system generate the required event logs or cover the Article 12(2)-(3) content, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Tying verifier identity to authenticated logs in an immutable store is a common, mundane response to this specific clause.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice using familiar identity and audit tools, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Authentication tokens tied to employee IDs and immutable audit logs are common, legally aligned practices that offend no norms (beyond routine employee-data considerations).
evidence_implementability: Integrating SSO/authentication tokens with a verification interface and an append-only store is routine engineering requiring modest, non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the Article 12(3)(d) requirement to identify natural persons verifying results, which is an explicit part of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, it would satisfy the verifier-identification element and timestamps, but it addresses only one of the several Article 12 logging requirements (e.g., reference database, input data, use periods, risk-event logging), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Auto-generating documentation from training runs is a fairly expected response to the documentation requirement, though a living dossier is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling for documentation but still treats compliance as a logging/documentation practice without changing how the lab does R&D.
evidence_acceptability: Automating compliance documentation from version control is a common, legally unobjectionable strategy that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It integrates into existing CI/CD and uses extractable metadata, requiring some tooling work but only non-radical changes to workflow.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Recital 71 technical documentation and traceability needs, though it addresses documentation more than the Article 12 event-logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help keep documentation current and audit-ready but does not itself provide automatic event logging of the deployed system under Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Experiment tracking and lineage tooling are well-known, so the idea is interesting in its compliance-as-reproducibility framing but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (middleware, ledger) and frames compliance as a reproducibility tool, but it still treats compliance essentially as logging practice rather than changing what or how the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Provenance tracking and experiment logging are common, uncontroversial practices that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building middleware that hashes inputs and logs to a centralized ledger is reasonably feasible with existing MLOps tools but requires some pipeline changes and engineering effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (development traceability and technical documentation per Recital 71) that relates to, but is not the same as, the stated need for automatic event logging over system lifetime.
evidence_effectiveness: Training lineage logging is reasonable and would help documentation and traceability, but Article 12 concerns runtime event logs of the deployed high-risk system (risk situations, post-market monitoring, operation monitoring), so it only partially solves the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Write-once tamper-proof log storage is a common, expected response to logging mandates and is not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging infrastructure that leaves the lab's R&D way of working and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Immutable audit storage is a common, widely accepted compliance strategy that violates no norms, though retention and deletion obligations such as GDPR need care.
evidence_implementability: WORM storage is mature off-the-shelf technology and linking it to an existing model registry via a pipeline requires some engineering changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: A WORM log archive directly addresses the logging and record-keeping mandate (Article 12) and its traceability purpose, though tamper-proofing is implied rather than explicitly required by the text.
evidence_effectiveness: It would secure and preserve logs for auditors but does not itself define which events to log or ensure the system automatically records relevant events, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: OAuth-based authenticated sign-off with audit logging is a standard, mundane approach to identity capture that any experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice implemented via existing identity tooling, leaving the lab's way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Authenticated reviewer logging is a common strategy that violates no norms, though handling personal identity data requires ordinary GDPR care.
evidence_implementability: Integrating OAuth identity management into internal validation tools and piping events to logs is straightforward, low-cost engineering with no radical change.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets an identified requirement within the stated problem (recording identity of verifiers under Article 12(3)(d)/14(5)), i.e., do X to get Y where Y is part of the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal would fully satisfy Article 12(3)(d) (identifying natural persons verifying results) but addresses only one of several logging requirements, so it is a partial solution to the overall logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Training workshops, checklists, templates and quarterly compliance audits are a very common, mundane response to regulatory mandates.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces some new process elements (templates, milestone checklists) but still treats compliance as a documentation practice, slightly stretching the paradigm at most.
evidence_acceptability: Training and checklist-based compliance are common strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Workshops, checklists and quarterly reviews are reasonably feasible with modest changes and existing staff.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (compliance process timing and technical documentation) related to the logging mandate rather than the automatic logging itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help embed documentation earlier but does not address automatic event logging required by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Testing suites for compliance logging are a mundane, expected response with little that is surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and QA practice that leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, treating compliance as logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing of logging against regulatory requirements is a common, uncontroversial engineering and compliance practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a test framework that simulates interactions and audits logs needs some engineering effort and requirements-to-test mapping, but it is reasonably feasible with existing tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying that Article 12 logs are correctly recorded.
evidence_effectiveness: It verifies logging correctness but does not itself implement logging or cover the full mandate (e.g., traceability appropriateness, documentation), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging SDKs/middleware are a very common and expected response to a logging mandate, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool but treats compliance purely as standard logging practice, leaving the lab's way of working essentially unchanged; at most a new tool element.
evidence_acceptability: A shared internal logging library is a common, uncontroversial engineering strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: A wrapper SDK built on existing telemetry tools is a modest, reasonably feasible engineering effort, though it requires some work to cover diverse architectures.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing required event types automatically.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute substantially to compliance by standardizing logging, but it captures only generic fields (timestamps, input references, session IDs) and does not address risk-relevant events, post-market monitoring, or Annex III specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated compliance-documentation pipelines (docs-as-code, model cards from CI) are a fairly common and expected response, showing little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as a documentation and logging practice, with the lab's research approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automating compliance documentation with CI/CD tooling is a common, uncontroversial practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Integrating CI/CD and version control to generate documentation is feasible with existing tooling, though mapping artifacts to regulatory requirements needs some custom work and process changes.
evidence_applicability: The idea directly addresses the documentation and record-keeping obligations tied to the logging mandate (Recital 71), though it targets technical documentation more than Article 12 event logs themselves.
evidence_effectiveness: Automated documentation generation would help keep technical documentation current but does not itself deliver the automatic event logging, traceability, or risk-event capture Article 12 requires, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reducing log storage overhead is a fairly predictable engineering response to a logging mandate, with only modest interest in the cryptographic hashing of reference database matches.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tools (compression and hashing research) but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing how the lab's R&D relates to its obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Reducing log storage cost while still keeping the mandated records violates no legal or social norms, though hashing in place of storing raw data could draw regulator scrutiny.
evidence_implementability: Compression and hashing of logs are established techniques that a lab can adopt with some engineering effort, though framing it as a research initiative adds some uncertainty and cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, the storage and compute cost of compliance logging, which relates to but is not the core stated problem of meeting the mandate or adapting R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: Cheaper log storage helps the lab bear the cost of logging but does not itself deliver the Article 12 capabilities such as event recording, traceability, or the Annex III minimums, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Auto-populating documentation from MLflow and version control is a common, widely expected approach to compliance documentation automation.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (parsers, templates) but still treats compliance as a documentation/record-keeping practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Automating documentation is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Parsing MLflow and version control metadata into templates uses existing tools and APIs and is reasonably easy to build at modest cost.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the technical documentation and record-keeping obligation in Recital 71, though it targets documentation rather than the Article 12 event logging mandate itself, making it an implied rather than identified match.
evidence_effectiveness: Auto-generated documentation synchronized with experiment trackers would help with the documentation upkeep requirement but does not provide automatic event logs over system lifetime, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Turning compliance logs into a scientific-discovery and forensic-debugging tool by correlating internal states with regulatory timestamps is unusual and shows some imagination, though interpretability logging is a known idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by weaving logging into the science of model understanding, which is paradigm stretching but does not change what the lab researches at large.
evidence_acceptability: Recording richer internal logs alongside mandatory events violates no legal or social norms, though it is somewhat unusual and may raise data-minimization or storage questions.
evidence_implementability: Capturing activations and attention weights at high-risk triggers requires new probes, large storage and overhead, and interpretability research that is difficult and expensive but not impossible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal links internal-state telemetry to Article 12 timestamps, which relates to the logging mandate, but it mainly solves an implied problem (interpretability and debugging) rather than directly meeting the specified logging requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with traceability and risk identification under Art. 12(2), but it is a research project that does not by itself guarantee the mandatory logs (e.g., Annex III usage periods, reference databases, persons involved), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Tying Article 12 logging to interpretable architectures with built-in reasoning logs is somewhat unusual and imaginative, but the interpretability-for-compliance link is a fairly familiar argument.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by making logging an intrinsic architectural research goal (compliance elevated to a frontier interpretability contribution), which stretches the paradigm, though it does not fundamentally redirect what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: A research initiative on interpretable architectures offends no legal or social norms and is consistent with regulatory goals, though framing compliance as research is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: Developing neural architectures with faithful, real-time structured reasoning logs is an open research problem requiring significant change and uncertain results, which is difficult though not impossible, and it is exploratory rather than a committed implementation.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the stated problem of how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D, but through an implied benefit (reasoning traces) rather than directly delivering the event logs Article 12 requires.
evidence_effectiveness: Even if achieved, reasoning logs would only partially satisfy Article 12, which concerns event recording for risk identification, post-market monitoring, and operation monitoring, so it contributes but is not a full solution.

evidence_originality: Log-based anomaly detection with dashboards is a common, expected response to monitoring requirements and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool (anomaly detection and dashboard) but still treats compliance as a logging and monitoring practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Monitoring dashboards and anomaly alerting are common, uncontroversial practices that violate no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building an anomaly detection layer and dashboard atop existing log streams requires some engineering work but uses standard tooling and is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses Article 12(2) purposes of identifying risk situations and supporting post-market monitoring, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with monitoring and risk-flagging but does not itself ensure the logging mandate is met (event capture, retention, Annex III specifics), so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using self-explaining architectures to produce semantic logs is an interesting and somewhat imaginative framing beyond event logging, but interpretability-for-traceability is a fairly familiar idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal links the lab's research agenda (interpretable architectures) to compliance, changing what the lab researches in response to traceability obligations, though it stops short of fully reorienting the lab.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing interpretability research and aligning with regulatory spirit violates no norms and is a common, welcome strategy in the research community.
evidence_implementability: Creating inherently self-explaining architectures that reliably log internal decision logic is an open research problem that requires significant effort and has uncertain results, making it difficult but not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (deeper traceability supporting the spirit of Article 12) rather than the explicit mandate to technically allow automatic event recording.
evidence_effectiveness: Research on interpretable logs would at best contribute to richer traceability in the long term and does not itself deliver Article 12's required automatic event logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Testing logs with mock audits is a sensible idea that experienced evaluators would expect, with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool and process (a sandbox and drills) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, with no change to how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Pre-certification testing and internal audit drills are sensible, uncontroversial practices that offend no norms.
evidence_implementability: It needs a dedicated test environment, a share of compute, simulated failures, and auditor-style drills, which is a reasonable but non-trivial set of changes.
evidence_applicability: The sandbox directly targets verifying that Article 12 logging captures risk-triggering events and supports traceability, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Compliance drills would reveal gaps in logging, but they only validate logging and do not build or specify it, so they are a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using a shared ontology of events to serve both legal traceability and scientific debugging, and predicting failure from logs, is unusual and imaginative, though not wholly unprecedented.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal turns compliance logging into a research contribution (open-source schema, legal-scientific ontology, logs as debugging and safety science), which changes the relationship between R&D and compliance without redefining what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: An open-source, cross-disciplinary standardization effort violates no norms and is broadly welcomed, though it is somewhat uncommon for a lab to do.
evidence_implementability: It requires cross-disciplinary teams, historical failure analysis, and community schema development, which is a significant and uncertain effort, though feasible with some changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses defining which events to log under Article 12(2) (risk situations, substantial modification), which is directly part of the logging mandate, though it is framed as research rather than direct compliance.
evidence_effectiveness: A schema of relevant events would help determine what to log but is only a partial solution, since it does not implement logging, retention, or the Annex III minimums, and its research outcome is uncertain.

evidence_originality: Automated log-verification tests using synthetic request flows as a release gate are a sensible but fairly expected engineering response to a logging mandate, with some interest but little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a test suite acting as a compliance gate) but still treats compliance as logging practice and does not change the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Automated testing of logging as a pre-release gate is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms or laws.
evidence_implementability: Building synthetic request tests and integrating them into release pipelines requires some effort across environments but is reasonably feasible using existing CI practices.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by verifying that required logging capabilities function before release.
evidence_effectiveness: It would verify that logs capture the required items such as start times and reference databases, but it does not itself create the logging or cover the broader Article 12 purposes like risk identification and monitoring, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated compliance documentation from MLOps metadata is a fairly common and expected idea, useful but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool but still treats compliance as a documentation/logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automating documentation from existing records is a common, uncontroversial compliance strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: The pipeline draws on existing tools (git, MLflow, DVC) and requires building a generator and flagging logic, which is reasonably feasible with some engineering effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the technical documentation requirement described in Recital 71, which is related to but only implied by the Article 12 logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help keep documentation current but does not implement automatic event logging of the system's operation required by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Data/model lineage tracking is a known MLOps practice, and the open-source metadata layer adds only a mildly interesting framing, so it is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a lineage metadata layer) and ties logging to scientific reproducibility, but it still treats compliance as logging practice without changing the lab's relationship to its obligations.
evidence_acceptability: An open-source internal metadata layer is a common, uncontroversial strategy, with only minor concerns about exposing sensitive data or IP.
evidence_implementability: Tracking every transformation across distributed clusters with absolute reproducibility is a significant engineering and storage burden, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: Lineage from training data to inference events relates to the traceability aim of Article 12, but the proposal never mentions the required event logging categories, so it addresses an implied problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute to traceability and logging of events but does not specify capture of Article 12(2) and 12(3) items such as use periods, reference databases, or verifier identities, so it only partially solves the mandate.

evidence_originality: Privacy-preserving logging is an interesting and somewhat unusual angle that shows some imagination, but differential privacy or MPC for logs is a fairly foreseeable response to the GDPR tension.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (cryptographic privacy techniques in the logging pipeline) but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing how the lab's R&D relates to its obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Protecting privacy while complying with the AI Act is a commonly accepted strategy that offends no norms, though the regulator-verification claim is slightly uncommon.
evidence_implementability: Embedding differential privacy or secure multi-party computation in a logging pipeline is technically demanding and costly, and differential privacy may conflict with exact-record requirements, so it is difficult but not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It solves an identified related problem, which is that mandatory logging of input data and user identities may conflict with privacy law, and this is part of the compliance challenge, though not the core logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It would address the GDPR conflict and support compliant logging, but it does not itself deliver the core logging capabilities required by Article 12, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Gating logging infrastructure on a risk classification in the pipeline is a sensible, fairly expected engineering response, with little surprise or imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new element (CI/CD triage that auto-enables logging modules) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Risk-tiered, pipeline-integrated compliance checklists are common practice and offend no norms, though the risk of misclassifying a system as low-risk is a minor concern.
evidence_implementability: Adding a checklist and conditional logging modules to an existing CI/CD pipeline is a reasonably feasible change, though building the logging modules and the classifier takes some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate only where legally required, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Triggering Article 12-compliant logging for high-risk projects would contribute to meeting the mandate, but it depends on correct risk classification and does not itself define what the logging must capture, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using logs for formal verification and near-miss anomaly detection, then publishing, is an interesting and somewhat imaginative idea, though 'compliance as research' is a fairly familiar framing and the proposal stays high-level.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between compliance and R&D by turning the logging obligation into a research program and scientific output, but it does not change what the lab fundamentally researches.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing research on safety and observability from compliance logs offends no norms, though disclosure of system logs may raise confidentiality or IP concerns.
evidence_implementability: Applying formal verification to real event logs of complex AI systems is difficult and expensive and requires specialist expertise, and the proposal is framed as exploratory research, but it is not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It uses the logs required by Article 12 to identify risk situations and near-misses, which relates to Article 12(2)(a), but it does not directly address how to meet the logging mandate itself, so it solves an implied problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute to risk identification and monitoring but does not by itself specify how to implement compliant logging, and proving absence of risk behaviors from logs is mathematically questionable, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A unified logging library with an immutable ledger is the standard, expected response from labs and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance tooling that treats the mandate as a logging practice and leaves the lab's research approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized compliance logging with immutable records is a common strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a modular API integrated with existing pipelines is reasonably feasible, though the immutable ledger and the cross-project integration require some engineering effort.
evidence_applicability: It does X (automatic standardized logging with Annex III templates) to get Y (Article 12 logging compliance), which is explicitly the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A standardized logging library capturing timestamps, inputs, and database references would, if built, directly satisfy the core Article 12 automatic-recording mandate, though it does not cover the technical documentation or other compliance duties.

evidence_originality: Mock audits and red-team style compliance testing are a familiar idea, though tracing decisions back to training data adds some interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A quarterly internal audit process is a new process element, but compliance is still treated as logging practice with no change to the lab's R&D.
evidence_acceptability: Internal review of compliance is a common, norm-respecting strategy that offends no one.
evidence_implementability: A quarterly review by a separate team is a modest process addition, though tracing decisions back to training data may be demanding and needs staffing.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets whether logs meet Article 12 traceability needs, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Audit simulations would catch gaps in logging but do not create the logging capability itself, so they only partly solve the problem.

evidence_originality: A centralized, reusable compliance logging library is a common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate and shows little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice (shared library with API hooks) that leaves the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized compliance tooling is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a modular library is a reasonable engineering task for a core team, though supporting diverse AI architectures requires some real effort and changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by providing automatic capture of timestamps, inputs, and user IDs.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared library would help with the core logging requirement but is only a partial solution, since it doesn't address event relevance for risk, post-market monitoring, Annex III specifics like reference databases, or retention.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging middleware is the obvious, common engineering response to a logging mandate, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared logging library is a new tool but still treats compliance as standard logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations, so it is slightly paradigm stretching at most.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized shared infrastructure for compliance is a standard, uncontroversial approach that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a common library and integrating it into the central cluster requires some engineering effort and researcher adoption but is reasonably feasible with existing infrastructure staff.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate by providing automatic event recording across projects.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic default capture of timestamps, inputs and versions would help meet Article 12 logging, but it does not cover all required events (risk situations, reference databases, human verifier identification) so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Unified observability wrappers with immutable logs are a fairly expected response, with the drift-analysis reuse adding only a modest interesting twist.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (wrapper, ledger) and reuses compliance logs for scientific drift analysis, but it still mainly treats compliance as logging practice, with only a mild nod to weaving it into the science.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized immutable logging for compliance is a common, norm-respecting strategy, though the ledger of all input/output pairs may raise minor data-privacy considerations.
evidence_implementability: Building a modular API wrapper and immutable centralized ledger across all R&D models requires some engineering changes but uses reasonably feasible, existing technology.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate for traceability, with an added benefit of scientific use.

evidence_acceptability: Automated logging for compliance is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Integrating a logging agent into deployment pipelines is reasonably feasible with some engineering work, though immutability and capturing system state add some effort.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate by automatically recording events.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially meet the logging requirement, but it is vague on event relevance to risk, post-market monitoring, and Annex III minimums such as identifying verifying persons, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance training programs are common and mundane, with only a minor twist in the combined metric and milestone tie-in.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance training, though a combined performance-and-traceability metric slightly stretches practice while still treating compliance as documentation/logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Mandatory internal training tied to approvals is a common, norm-compliant corporate compliance strategy.
evidence_implementability: Monthly workshops and milestone gating are easy and low-cost to set up, requiring only modest process changes.
evidence_applicability: Training researchers on documentation and event-log requirements addresses the stated problem of adapting R&D to the logging mandate, though via an implied route (awareness) rather than directly building logging.
evidence_effectiveness: Training and milestone gating would help build compliance culture but does not itself implement automatic logging capabilities, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Recording human verifier identity is exactly what Article 12(3)(d) prescribes, so the idea is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a new tool but treats compliance purely as logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Logging reviewer identities with authentication is a standard, legally aligned compliance practice that offends no norms (though staff-tracking privacy is a minor consideration).
evidence_implementability: Adding an authentication and timestamp layer to internal evaluation tools is a modest, non-radical change with low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12(3)(d) requirement to log identities of natural persons verifying results, which is part of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It covers only one sub-item of the Annex III point 1(a) logging minimums and not the general Article 12 logging requirements, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Internal budget set-asides for compliance overhead are a fairly common, mundane administrative response and not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a funding mechanism but treats compliance as an overhead cost of logging, leaving the lab's R&D and compliance relationship essentially unchanged, though the budget process is a slight new element.
evidence_acceptability: Internal budget allocation for compliance costs is a common strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Setting aside a budget percentage and an application process is a non-radical administrative change that is easy to implement at low cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, the cost burden of logging storage and compute, which relates to the stated problem but not directly to how to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help pay for logging infrastructure but does nothing to build the logging capability or ensure Article 12 compliance, so it is only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Benchmarking which log data points matter and publishing open benchmarks is somewhat interesting and goes beyond plain compliance, but it is a fairly expected research-and-thought-leadership response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new elements (comparative studies, open benchmarks) and a research angle, yet still treats compliance as a logging practice and does not change how the lab's R&D relates to its obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing open benchmarks and studying logs is a common, norm-abiding strategy, though using existing system logs may raise minor data-access or confidentiality questions.
evidence_implementability: Comparative studies across domains require access to logs from various high-risk systems and a developed metric methodology, which is a significant, somewhat difficult effort but feasible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, knowing what logging is actually useful for post-market monitoring, which relates to the mandate but is not the lab's direct need to implement logging.
evidence_effectiveness: The benchmarks would help identify useful log data but do not themselves make the lab's systems compliant with the logging mandate, so they are only a partial contribution.

evidence_originality: Hash-linking logs to versioned reference data is a sensible, somewhat imaginative idea but a fairly expected engineering response to the Article 12(3)(b) requirement.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new tool (versioned database snapshots linked to log entries) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, so it is slightly paradigm stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Versioning and hashing data is a common, norm-compliant data engineering practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Git-like or snapshot versioning tools exist, but snapshotting large or changing databases and linking to every log entry requires some pipeline changes and storage cost.
evidence_applicability: It explicitly addresses an identified requirement in the stated problem (Article 12(3)(b) reference database recording), so X directly yields a Y that is part of the problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would solve one specific element (identifying the reference database) but not the whole logging mandate, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Experiment tracking and lineage tooling (e.g., MLflow-style) is a well-known approach, so this is a fairly expected response with little surprising about it.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a unified tooling layer and ties compliance logs to research reproducibility, but still treats compliance primarily as logging practice with a modest dual benefit.
evidence_acceptability: Automated provenance and logging is a common, norm-compatible compliance and MLOps strategy with no legal or social objections.
evidence_implementability: Integrating metadata hooks into core training frameworks and building a queryable lineage database is a moderate engineering effort similar to existing MLOps tooling, requiring some changes but being reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the Article 12 logging mandate by capturing required event logs plus lineage, which is part of the stated problem of meeting the logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, automated capture of event logs, datasets, and system states in a queryable store would substantially satisfy traceability and logging, though it does not specify Article 12(2) event relevance or Annex III 3 minimums, so it is a strong but not fully specified solution.

evidence_originality: A periodic review board for logs is a common governance response that an experienced evaluator would expect from most labs.

evidence_effectiveness: A quarterly log review board addresses Article 12(2) purposes (risk identification, post-market and operational monitoring) but does not itself implement the logging mandate or the Annex III minimum fields, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Privacy-preserving logs via ZK proofs and MPC are interesting and show some imagination, but privacy-vs-logging tension is a known topic that experienced evaluators would expect from some labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (cryptographic log tools) and frames compliance as a competitive advantage, but still treats compliance fundamentally as a logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-enhancing logging research is legally and socially acceptable and offends no sensibilities, though it is somewhat less common than plain logging.
evidence_implementability: Prototyping zero-knowledge proofs and secure multi-party computation in existing architectures is difficult, costly, and uncertain, and the proposal is explicitly exploratory ('test feasibility'), which conflicts with the commitment-not-exploration criterion.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied related problem (making logs compliant while protecting personal data) rather than the directly stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Privacy-preserving logs would address a real tension with GDPR but a research project does not itself deliver the Article 12 logging capability, so it contributes only partially to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Auto-generating docs from experiment trackers is a well-known MLOps practice and an expected response, so it is mundane rather than ingenious.

evidence_originality: Using counterfactual probes to log why alternatives were not chosen is an interesting, somewhat imaginative framing, though 'compliance as interpretability opportunity' is a fairly foreseeable response.

evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate and traceability by proposing richer logs, though the causal-trigger focus goes beyond the stated minimum requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: Richer causal logs would contribute to traceability and risk identification, but the approach is speculative, does not ensure baseline Article 12 compliance by itself, and is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using internal activations and attention maps as regulatory logs is interesting and shows some imagination, though interpretability-for-audit ideas are known in the literature and the proposal is fairly generic.

evidence_acceptability: Automating documentation from version control is a common, norm-compliant approach that offends no legal or social sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Linking version control, datasets, and validation outputs to a documentation engine requires some tooling and integration work but is reasonably feasible with existing technology.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Recital 71 technical documentation requirement, but Article 12 mandates automatic event logs, so it targets a closely related implied problem rather than the logging mandate itself.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with documentation and audit-readiness but does not provide the event-level logging required by Article 12, so it is only a partial solution, and the claim of eliminating human error is overstated.

evidence_originality: A shared logging library or module is the obvious and mundane response that most labs would propose.

evidence_effectiveness: A centralized logging library capturing timestamps, reference database use, and user identification would meet most of Article 12's technical logging mandate, but it does not address which events matter for risk, post-market monitoring, or retention, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_acceptability: Internal milestone reviews and compliance checklists are common strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding a checklist and a single reviewer to existing milestone reviews is a non-radical, low-cost change, though reliance on one lead architect is a modest bottleneck.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of ensuring systems meet the Article 12 logging mandate by checking compliance before deployment.
evidence_effectiveness: A checklist gate would help verify that logging capability exists before deployment but does not itself build the logging or specify what must be recorded, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A logging middleware with decorators and API gateway plugins writing to an immutable store is the most common, expected engineering response to an automatic logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice wrapped around existing services, leaving the lab's R&D approach and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized logging middleware is a common, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms, though storing input data may raise minor privacy considerations.
evidence_implementability: Building Python decorators and gateway plugins over existing services is reasonably feasible with moderate engineering effort, though a centralized immutable database adds some infrastructure work.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (automatic immutable logging middleware) to get Y (Article 12 logging capability), which is explicitly the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic, consistent event logging would address the core Article 12 mandate, but it does not cover the Article 12(2) event-relevance purposes or the Annex III 1(a) specific fields such as reference database and verifier identity, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Validating logging through synthetic failure scenarios is a sensible, fairly familiar testing practice (like fault injection or audit testing) that shows only modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a simulation environment) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal testing of logging systems with synthetic data violates no norms and is a common, uncontroversial compliance-assurance strategy.
evidence_implementability: Building a synthetic scenario test environment requires some engineering effort and domain definition of risk scenarios but is reasonably feasible with existing testing skills.
evidence_applicability: The suite directly targets validating the Article 12(2)(a) risk-identification logs, which is an identified part of the logging mandate the lab must meet.
evidence_effectiveness: Testing with synthetic failure scenarios would help verify that risk logging works, but it covers only one sub-requirement (12(2)(a)) and not the other logging duties (12(2)(b), 12(2)(c), retention, Annex III minimums), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Low-overhead logging is an expected response to the mandate, though semantic hashing of activations and risk-threshold triggers add some interest.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new technical tools but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing the lab's relation to its obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Building efficient logging that supports compliance is a common, legally unobjectionable strategy, though selective/sampled logging could raise mild questions about completeness.
evidence_implementability: It requires a research effort on compression, selective activation tracing and semantic hashing for large networks, which is difficult and uncertain rather than a ready measure, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified problem of meeting the automatic logging mandate without hurting performance, so doing X yields Y which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Efficient logging would help meet Article 12 while preserving performance, but it addresses only the technical part and sampled logging may not satisfy the traceability requirements, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A centralized, automatic, immutable logging layer is a well-expected response for labs facing a logging mandate, with the reproducibility side benefit being only mildly interesting.

evidence_acceptability: Provenance tracking and versioned data stores are common practices that offend no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a versioned data lake with automatic linking to Git and dataset hashes requires some engineering changes but uses existing tools and is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate by linking Article 12 event logs to traceable model versions and also supports research reproducibility.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially support traceability but does not itself define which events to log, cover Article 12(3) specifics, or address retention, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Centralized logging middleware with decorators that auto-capture events is a very common engineering response to logging mandates, so it is mundane rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (middleware/decorators) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and explicitly keeps R&D unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Standard observability tooling raises no legal, social, or business objections and fits normal engineering practice.
evidence_implementability: Building wrappers and a central time-series database across all projects requires some engineering effort and integration but is reasonably feasible with existing technology.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of how to meet the logging mandate (automatic recording of events) while preserving R&D speed.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic event capture would meet the core Article 12 logging capability for many systems, but it does not cover Annex III-specific fields, documentation, or deciding which events are relevant, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Linking activation-level causal tracing to regulatory log entries is somewhat unusual and shows imagination, though interpretability-for-compliance is a recognizable idea.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance logging as a research contribution woven into interpretability science, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, but it does not alter what the lab researches at large.
evidence_acceptability: Interpretability-based logging is an unusual but reputable approach that offends no legal or social norms, though it may raise concerns about overhead and exposing model internals.
evidence_implementability: Real-time causal tracing of internal activations during inference is an open research problem that is expensive and difficult, and the proposal is framed as research rather than a committed implementation, though not totally impossible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal targets how to meet the logging mandate by turning event logs into semantic traces, but Article 12 asks for event recording for traceability and monitoring, not explanations of decisions, so it solves an implied related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Semantic traces would contribute to traceability and risk identification, but they are only a partial solution because they do not cover the basic logging requirements such as use periods, reference databases and reviewer identification, and mapping activations to log entries is unlikely to work reliably.

evidence_originality: Experiment-tracking and provenance ledgers (MLflow-style) are what labs routinely propose, so this is common and mundane, though the reproducibility tie-in is mildly interesting.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a tooling layer but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Automated logging and provenance tracking is a common, norm-compliant strategy that offends no legal or social sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Integrating hooks into existing ML libraries and clusters plus a versioned database requires some engineering changes but is reasonably feasible with existing tooling.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by automatically capturing events and metadata.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute substantially to Article 12 compliance, but it captures training-time metadata rather than the deployed system's runtime events and specific Article 12(2)-(3) content, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A classification checklist with periodic compliance reviews is a very common, expected governance response to the mandate, showing little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance process (screening and review) that leaves the lab's way of working and its relation to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Internal checklists and compliance reviews are common strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A pre-development checklist and quarterly reviews by existing compliance staff and scientists are low-cost, non-radical changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified need to know which logging requirements apply to which systems, which is directly part of deciding how to meet the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It only determines which Article 12 requirements apply and does not itself build logging capability, so it contributes to but only partially solves the problem.

evidence_originality: A capital expenditure request for log storage with a cost-benefit analysis is a common, mundane organizational response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as a standard infrastructure cost line item and leaves the lab's R&D approach and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Requesting budget through a cost-benefit analysis to a funding board is a standard practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Preparing and presenting a budget request is easy, though the approval and procurement of storage and compute capacity involve some cost and effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem (funding the infrastructure needed to retain logs) that relates to the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Securing a budget for storage and compute for log retention helps fund the logging mandate but does not itself design or implement logging, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A shared logging library/middleware with a consistent API is the most common and expected engineering response to a logging mandate, so it is mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as standard logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D way of working essentially unchanged, merely centralizing the tooling.
evidence_acceptability: Standardized internal logging tooling is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Building an internal logging library and middleware and embedding it in project templates is a reasonably feasible engineering task with moderate cost, though retrofitting active pipelines needs some changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by automating event recording across the lab's systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute substantially to meeting Article 12's automatic logging requirement, but it covers only basic events (timestamps, input hashes, user IDs) and not risk-relevant events, post-market monitoring needs, or Annex III specifics like reference databases, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Reconstruction drills as audit are an adaptation of familiar internal audit and penetration-testing ideas, interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a new process element (stress tests) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Internal audit drills are a recognized, uncontroversial compliance practice that offends no norms, though the 'fire drill' framing is slightly unusual.
evidence_implementability: A quarterly internal audit using existing logs and the compliance office requires some process setup and researcher time but no radical changes or major new infrastructure.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets whether the logs meet the traceability and post-market monitoring purposes of the logging mandate, solving an identified part of the stated problem (verifying logging adequacy).
evidence_effectiveness: It would verify and remediate log quality but does not itself create the logging capability or cover all mandate aspects, so it is a helpful partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using compliance logging as a research object for failure prediction and publication is somewhat unusual and shows some imagination, but is not strikingly surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It turns logging from passive compliance into an active diagnostic and publishable research output, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations by weaving logging into the science.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing peer-reviewed research and analyzing logs is a norm-compatible approach, though somewhat uncommon as a compliance response.
evidence_implementability: It requires a dedicated research project and historical logs that may not exist for such purposes, and research outcomes are uncertain, making it a significant but feasible undertaking.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how to determine which events to log under Article 12 (identifying risk situations, monitoring), which is part of meeting the logging mandate, though it frames itself as research.
evidence_effectiveness: A taxonomy of predictive events would help the lab decide what to log for Article 12 but would not itself implement logging or ensure compliance, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A reviewer sign-off dashboard that logs reviewer identity is an expected response to Article 12(3)(d), though reusing the decisions as ground-truth data for model refinement adds a mildly interesting twist.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a review UI) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, so the lab's relationship between R&D and compliance is not changed.
evidence_acceptability: Human oversight sign-off with audit trails is a common, norm-compatible practice, with only minor reviewer-privacy considerations.
evidence_implementability: A lightweight dashboard capturing reviewer identity and decision alongside log entries is a modest build with standard tooling and no radical organizational change.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets an identified requirement in Article 12(3)(d), which is part of the stated logging problem, though that requirement applies only to Annex III 1(a) systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would satisfy the reviewer-identification requirement of 12(3)(d) but covers only one sub-item of the broader logging mandate (periods of use, reference database, matched inputs, risk events), so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A log-validation tool that checks logs against Article 12 fields is a common, expected compliance-tooling response with little that is surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (validation scripts) but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing how R&D relates to obligations, fitting level 2.
evidence_acceptability: Internal compliance checking tooling is a common strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Writing validation scripts and an automated checklist against known log fields is low-cost and non-radical for a lab.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of verifying that logging meets the Article 12 mandate, with the output (gap detection) part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help detect logging gaps but does not itself implement logging or address risk-event relevance or Annex III-specific items, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A centralized logging middleware library is a common, mundane engineering response that evaluators would expect from most labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool but treats compliance purely as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D approach unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Standardized internal tooling for compliance violates no norms and is a common strategy.
evidence_implementability: Building middleware hooks that integrate with existing clusters requires some engineering effort and researcher adoption but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by building a standard library that captures inputs, timestamps and verification IDs.
evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging library would substantially deliver automatic logging across projects, but it is a partial solution because it does not specify event relevance to risk, post-market monitoring, retention, or the Annex III-specific fields like reference databases.

evidence_originality: Using mandated logs as a longitudinal robustness research dataset is an unusual and interesting angle that shows some imagination but is not startling.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance logs as a primary research data source feeding model safety refinement, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance, though it stops short of changing what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Using deployment telemetry for research is somewhat uncommon and raises data-sharing and privacy concerns with deployers, but it does not offend sensibilities if governed properly.
evidence_implementability: A secure telemetry loop with deployers, access to their logs, and a longitudinal study require significant cooperation, infrastructure, and cost, though they are not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied problem, getting research value from compliance logging, which relates to adapting R&D to the mandate but not directly to meeting the logging requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: It would not itself deliver the Article 12 logging capability and relies on logs existing, so it contributes only partially by exploiting logs for research value.

evidence_originality: Standardized logging wrappers or SDKs are a very common and mundane response that an evaluator would expect from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged beyond reducing friction.
evidence_acceptability: Shared internal logging libraries are a common engineering strategy that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building an internal library with hooks into existing ML frameworks is a routine engineering effort requiring modest changes and cost.
evidence_applicability: The shared logging library directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate (start/end times, input metadata) across R&D prototypes.
evidence_effectiveness: A standardized middleware would contribute substantially to automatic event recording but covers only basic fields and does not address traceability relevance, retention, reference databases, or risk-event identification, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Data lineage with content hashing is a well-known and expected response to this mandate, so it is mundane despite being sensible.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a tooling layer (version control, hashing) but still treats compliance as a logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Immutable, hash-based audit logging is a conventional compliance-friendly approach that violates no norms, though immutability may raise data-retention and erasure questions.
evidence_implementability: Dataset version control and hashing are mature tools, but real-time linkage to each inference and integration into the logging pipeline require some engineering changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the identified requirements in Article 12(3)(b) and (c) directly, so X (hash-linked lineage logs) produces Y (the mandated records), which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Versioned dataset hashes tied to input matches would satisfy the Annex III 1(a) reference-database and matched-input logging items, but they leave out use-period timestamps, human verifier identification, and the broader Article 12(2) event logging, so the fix is only partial.

evidence_originality: Using empirical study to ground which events to log is sensible and somewhat interesting but not highly surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new element (an event taxonomy) but still treats compliance as a logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A research study to define loggable risk events is a common, norm-compliant approach that offends no legal or social sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Analyzing failure modes across existing systems and building a taxonomy requires dedicated research effort and data access, but it is reasonably feasible with moderate changes.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the identified need to determine which events are relevant for logging under Article 12(2), which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: A taxonomy of relevant events would help satisfy Article 12(2) by clarifying what to log, but it is only a partial solution since it does not build the logging capability itself.

evidence_originality: Periodic compliance audits against a checklist are a common, mundane response expected from most labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Quarterly internal audits with a checklist are standard compliance practice that leaves the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
