evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a tooling pipeline but still treats compliance as logging practice, though the reproducibility tie-in slightly weaves it into the science, so it is slightly stretching.
evidence_acceptability: Standard engineering practice that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: MLflow, git and data snapshotting are mature, widely used tools that a lab can adopt with modest changes and cost.
evidence_applicability: It addresses traceability and logging of runs, which relates directly to the logging mandate, though Article 12 concerns events during operation of deployed systems rather than R&D provenance, so the fit is partly implied.
evidence_effectiveness: It contributes to traceability and versioning but does not cover event logging for risk identification, post-market monitoring, operation monitoring, or Annex III specifics, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Docs-as-code and auto-generated documentation from docstrings are common and mundane approaches, with the 'living ledger' label adding little new.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a tooling and process improvement that still treats compliance as a documentation or logging practice without changing how R&D relates to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Automating documentation from code is a common, uncontroversial practice that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Docstring parsing and version-control hooks are existing, inexpensive tooling that fits normal developer workflows, though real-time generation of complete documentation needs some setup.
evidence_applicability: It targets technical documentation (Recital 71) which is related to but not the Article 12 logging mandate itself, so it solves an implied, related problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Auto-generated docs from code comments would help keep documentation current but do not provide event logging or cover the content needed for risk management, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Signed human-verification logs are a fairly common and mundane compliance approach, with little that is surprising or imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a digital signature tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D way of working essentially intact, which is slight stretching at most.
evidence_acceptability: Logging who verified outputs through signed identity records is a standard, uncontroversial accountability practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Linking digital signatures to an existing internal identity provider and adding it to the validation stage requires some integration work but is reasonably feasible at modest cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the Article 12(3)(d) requirement to identify natural persons involved in verification, which is part of the logging mandate, though that clause applies only to Annex III 1(a) systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would satisfy one narrow logging item but leaves automatic event logging, risk-related events, post-market monitoring, and other Article 12 requirements unaddressed, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Automated experiment tracking with immutable records is a common, familiar response (similar to existing MLOps tools), so it is interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a new tool (a provenance library) but still treats compliance as a logging practice, with a modest nod to reproducibility benefits.
evidence_acceptability: Open-source provenance tooling and reproducibility logging are common strategies that violate no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Integrating a modular library into existing ML pipelines is reasonably feasible with some engineering changes, and immutable records add moderate effort.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of traceability and documentation related to logging, but not the explicit operation-time event logging for risk, post-market monitoring, and deployer monitoring.
evidence_effectiveness: Article 12 concerns runtime event logging of the deployed system, whereas this captures training-run provenance, so it would only partially contribute to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Data versioning with cryptographic hashing for provenance is a common, expected response, showing little imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard logging practice embedded in the existing pipeline and does not change how the lab relates R&D to compliance.
evidence_acceptability: Automated logging with hashing and versioning of data is a standard, legally compliant engineering practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires modest changes to the data loading layer and metadata recording, which are reasonably feasible with existing tools, though per-inference logging adds some overhead.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets an identified part of the stated problem, meeting the logging mandate for reference database and traceability.
evidence_effectiveness: It would address the reference-database logging element of Article 12(3) and general traceability, but it covers only part of the mandate (e.g., use periods, input matches, reviewer identities, risk-event logging).

evidence_originality: A dedicated module for Annex III 1(a) logging with immutable ledgering is a fairly expected response, with only slight interest from the ledger element.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal adds a recording module with immutable ledgering but treats compliance purely as a logging practice, leaving the lab's R&D way of working unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Immutable ledgering of personnel identities raises some data protection and worker privacy concerns (GDPR, retention and erasure conflicts), though it is a legally mandated and common compliance approach.
evidence_implementability: Building a logging module with tamper-evident storage is reasonably feasible with existing technology, though it requires some engineering changes and integration work.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an identified problem, the Article 12(3) logging items (match data, reference database, verifier identities, use periods), which is directly part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would directly satisfy the Article 12(3) minimum logging requirements for remote biometric identification systems, but it does not cover the general Article 12(1)-(2) logging mandate across other high-risk systems, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A centralized, standardized logging library with an immutable store is the obvious engineering response that most labs would propose, so it is common and mundane.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: A shared middleware logging library is a new tool but still treats compliance as a logging practice kept separate from research, so the lab's way of working is unchanged in relationship terms.
evidence_acceptability: Centralized automated compliance logging is a standard, uncontroversial strategy that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Building middleware that hooks into existing training and deployment pipelines and a centralized immutable database requires some engineering changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate by automatically capturing timestamps, reference databases, and input data as Article 12 requires.
evidence_effectiveness: It would substantially deliver automatic event recording, but it does not by itself address risk-relevant event identification, post-market monitoring, or Article 12(3) specifics like human verifier identification, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Using Prometheus and Grafana for log-based alerting is a common observability practice, and applying it to Article 79 risk metrics is only a mildly interesting framing.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tooling (Prometheus/Grafana alerts) but still treats compliance as logging practice and leaves the lab's R&D relationship to compliance largely unchanged, though it does tie logs to validation cycles.
evidence_acceptability: Monitoring dashboards over logs are a standard, uncontroversial strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Prometheus and Grafana are mature open-source tools, though defining Article 79 risk metrics and correlating logs with degradation markers requires some custom work.
evidence_applicability: The dashboard directly targets Article 12(2)(a) by flagging log anomalies that indicate risk or substantial modification, which is part of the logging mandate, though it does not itself address the core recording requirements.
evidence_effectiveness: A monitoring dashboard helps use logs for risk identification and post-market monitoring but does not ensure the automatic recording, log content, or Annex III minimums, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Encrypted ledgers for sensitive logs are an interesting and sensible idea but fairly expected among compliance responses, with limited surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (encrypted ledger, privacy-preserving protocols) and gestures at competitive advantage, but still treats compliance primarily as a logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Privacy-preserving logging for compliance is a legally and socially unobjectionable approach, though a bespoke research initiative is somewhat unusual.
evidence_implementability: Building a custom encrypted ledger with a cross-functional team of cryptographers and engineers is a significant, costly undertaking, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets the Article 12(3) minimum logging requirements (reference database, input matches, verifier identities) for Annex III 1(a) systems, which are part of the stated logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: An encrypted, privacy-preserving ledger that records these Article 12(3) items would meet the specific logging mandate if built, but it covers only the Annex III 1(a) subset and not the general Article 12(1)-(2) logging or documentation needs.

evidence_originality: Embedding decision-path tracing in the architecture is an unusual and somewhat imaginative framing, though interpretable-architecture research is a known area.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It folds traceability into the model architecture and the science itself, changing how R&D relates to compliance rather than just adding a logging tool.
evidence_acceptability: Exploring explainable architectures offends no norms, though presenting it as meeting the spirit of the regulation is somewhat unusual and regulators may not accept it as compliance.
evidence_implementability: It is an open-ended research study with uncertain outcomes that would require significant R&D change and is not a deployable measure, though not impossible.
evidence_applicability: It addresses an implied related problem (traceability and explainability of model behavior) rather than the identified logging mandate, so it applies only indirectly to the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Article 12 requires automatic event logs (period of use, reference database, input data, reviewers), and latent-space reasoning traces from an exploratory study would not produce those records, so it is unlikely to solve the compliance problem.

evidence_originality: A centralized logging library/middleware with standardized API hooks is the most common, expected engineering response to a logging mandate.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance and logging practice that leaves the lab's research workflow and its relationship to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Building shared internal tooling to meet a legal requirement is a common strategy that offends no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Integrating a plug-and-play module into existing training pipelines requires some engineering effort but is reasonably feasible and non-radical.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the stated problem of meeting Article 12's automatic event-logging mandate by producing the logs.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help deliver automatic logging and timestamps, but the proposal is vague on Article 12's specific event-content requirements, retention, and Annex III minimums, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A centralized logging middleware/API is a common, mundane response expected from labs facing Article 12.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats compliance as a standard logging infrastructure practice and leaves the lab's research way of working unchanged, though it is a new tool.
evidence_acceptability: A shared logging middleware maintained by DevOps is a conventional compliance approach that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a plug-and-play layer across all architectures requires some engineering and integration changes but is reasonably feasible with existing DevOps resources.
evidence_applicability: It directly does X (automatic logging middleware) to get Y (meeting Article 12 technical logging requirements), which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic event logging directly addresses the Article 12 mandate, but the proposal is generic and does not address risk-relevant event selection, retention, or Annex III specifics, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Version-controlled documentation with milestone gates is a common, expected response to documentation mandates and shows little surprise.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a version-controlled vault and milestone-integrated checks, but still treats compliance as a documentation/logging practice without changing what or how the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Internal documentation requirements for researchers are standard and offend no norms or legal sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Version control tools and milestone checks are cheap and readily available, though researcher discipline requires some process change.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the technical documentation concern in Recital 71, which relates to the regulation but only implicitly to Article 12's automatic event logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It would help with documentation and audit readiness but does not provide automatic event logs of system operation, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Risk classification and scoping audits are the mundane, expected first step for most labs facing the Act.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is a standard compliance scoping exercise that leaves the lab's way of working and its view of compliance as logging practice unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Triaging projects by risk category with compliance workshops is a common, lawful, uncontroversial practice that offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Review workshops between researchers and the compliance officer are low-cost and need only non-radical process changes.
evidence_applicability: Determining which systems are high-risk and need Article 12 logging directly addresses the question of how to meet the logging mandate efficiently, though it does not itself build logging.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps by targeting resources correctly but implements no logging capability, so it is only a partial solution to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Empirically studying minimum logging granularity needed to detect risks is interesting and somewhat unusual, but not especially surprising or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements (ablation studies on logging granularity, a published standard) and turns compliance into a research output, which stretches the relationship between R&D and compliance somewhat but still centers on logging.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing research and proposing standards violates no norms and is a common, legitimate academic and industry strategy.
evidence_implementability: Ablation studies and publication are feasible with existing research staff, but defining a minimal sufficient information set for systemic risk detection is open-ended, requires some resources, and does not deliver a compliant logging system, so it is reasonably feasible only with some changes.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the implied problem of what 'appropriate' traceability means under Article 12(2), which relates to the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate, rather than directly delivering logging.
evidence_effectiveness: Defining and quantifying adequate traceability could inform how to meet Article 12(2), but it is a research and standard-setting effort that does not itself implement logging, so it only partially solves the lab's decision problem.

evidence_originality: Compliance stage gates and checklists are a very common, mundane response that an experienced evaluator would expect.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance practice added to existing processes and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A stage-gate checklist and peer review for compliance is a common, norm-conforming governance practice that offends no sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding a checklist and peer-review gate to an existing milestone process requires some process changes but is reasonably feasible and low cost.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets the stated problem of meeting the Article 12 logging mandate within R&D by verifying logging capabilities before validation.
evidence_effectiveness: It helps catch gaps early but only verifies logging rather than designing it or addressing the substance of what to log, so it is a partial solution.

evidence_originality: Compliance-as-code checks in CI/CD are a common and expected response, making this mundane rather than surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a tool to the pipeline but treats compliance as standard logging practice and leaves the lab's way of working essentially unchanged, though shifting left adds a slight new element.
evidence_acceptability: A CI/CD compliance gate is a widely accepted engineering practice that violates no legal, social or business norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a pipeline check for logging hooks needs some development and integration work but uses existing CI/CD tooling, so it is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the identified problem of meeting the logging mandate by checking required fields are present before deployment.
evidence_effectiveness: It would verify that logging hooks exist, which helps with Article 12 but does not itself ensure log content adequacy, retention, or the traceability purposes, so it is only a partial solution.

evidence_originality: A unified logging wrapper is a common, mundane response that experienced evaluators would expect from most labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It is standard compliance logging practice implemented as a tool, leaving the lab's way of working and its relation to compliance unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: A centralized compliance logging module is a common strategy that violates no legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a standardized internal logging library or API wrapper and integrating it across pipelines requires some engineering changes but is a reasonably feasible, standard software measure.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the logging mandate by automating event recording to meet Article 12, which is part of the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: It would contribute substantially to meeting Article 12 but is only partial, since it does not address the risk-relevant event selection, retention, or non-Annex III specifics and assumes the wrapper captures what is needed.
